English

Pronunciation

  • IPA(key): /dɛm/
    • Audio (Southern England):(file)
  • Rhymes: -ɛm

Pronoun

dem

  1. Nonstandard form of them.
    • 2007 February 25, Sia Michel, “Stephen Marley in Tallahassee, M.I.A. in India and Klaxons on Fire”, in The New York Times‎, New York, N.Y.: The New York Times Company, →ISSN, →OCLC, archived from the original on 4 November 2025:
      Go tell dem natty dreadlocks no wear handcuff,” advises Damian Marley, his guest star and younger brother, who accuses the officers of jealousy.

Determiner

dem

  1. Nonstandard form of them, in the sense of "those".
    What are dem fings doing ’ere?
  2. (Caribbean, Jamaica, MLE, slang) (clitic, suffix) A group of.
    • 1956, “Give Her Love”, performed by Chin’s Calypso Sextet:
      Love tenderness is what the woman dem want
    • 2009, Dizzee Rascal, “Chillin' Wiv Da Man Dem”:
      Chillin' wiv da man dem
      Jammin' wiv da man dem
      It's all good in the hood wiv da man dem
    • 2010, Plan B, “Stay Too Long”:
      I’ve got my peeps dem with me shouting pull up your socks,
      Cos we just broke the law and now we're running from cops.

Derived terms

  • gyal dem

Anagrams

  • D. Me., DME, EDM, Edm, MEd, Med, Med., med

Albanian

Etymology

From Proto-Albanian *dama, from Proto-Indo-European *dm̥h₂ós (“bull”) (compare Irish damh, Ancient Greek δάμαλος (dámalos, “calf”)), from *demh₂- (“to tame”) (compare Latin domō, English tame).[1]

Pronunciation

  • Audio:(file)

Noun

dem m (plural dema, definite demi, definite plural demat)

  1. bull
  2. main load-bearing beam in a floor

        Norwegian Bokmål

        Pronunciation

        • IPA(key): /dɛm/, [dɛmː]
        • (unstressed pronoun) IPA(key): /dɛm/, [dɛm]
        • Rhymes: -ɛm
        • Homophone: Dem
        • Hyphenation: dem

        Etymology 1

        PIE word
        *só

        Inherited from Middle Norwegian þæim (“them”), attested in a document from 1409,[1] from Old Norse þeim (“them; those”), the dative plural of sá (“that”), from Proto-Germanic *þaimaz, its dative plural, from Proto-Indo-European *tóymos, the masculine and neuter dative/ablative plural of *só (“that”). The former dative became the general object form.

        Compare dialectal Norwegian Nynorsk deim, Danish dem, Swedish dem, Icelandic þeim, Faroese teimum and English them (“them”); the English form was borrowed from Old Norse through Middle English.

        Pronoun

        dem (nominative de, possessive deres)

        1. them; the third-person plural object pronoun, referring to people, animals or things.
          Jeg møtte dem på stasjonen. ― I met them at the station.
          Vi ga dem litt mat. ― We gave them some food.
          Jeg snakket med dem i går. ― I spoke with them yesterday.
          og dem — (colloquial, especially after a personal name) and the others associated with that person.
          Vi skal besøke Per og dem i helgen. ― We're going to visit Per and the others this weekend.
          • 1873, Henrik Ibsen, Kærlighedens komedie, page 112:
            bøgerne, – dem kan du selv beholde
            The books—you can keep them yourself.
          • 1874, Henrik Ibsen, Peer Gynt, page 12:
            hvor er skæpperne med mynt efter gamle Rasmus Gynt; faer din gav dem fødder, han
            Where are the bushels of coins left by old Rasmus Gynt? Your father gave them legs, he did.
          • 1882, Jonas Lie, Gaa paa!, page 152:
            jeg har velstaaende familje, – om jeg vilde ulejlige dem
            I have well-to-do family—if I cared to trouble them.
          • 1888, Henrik Ibsen, Fruen fra havet, page 214:
            vel kan du holde mig tilbage her! … Men mit sind, – alle mine tanker … dem kan du ikke binde!
            You may keep me here! … But my mind—all my thoughts … you cannot bind them!
          • 1891, Arne Garborg, Trætte Mænd, page 53:
            de, som stjæler i stort, dem faar man uvilkaarlig en vis agtelse for
            Those who steal on a grand scale—one cannot help feeling a certain respect for them.
          • 1896, Henrik Ibsen, John Gabriel Borkman, page 7:
            [det var] bare nogen penge – eller nogen papirer, – som det gik ud over for dem. Men for os –!
            [It was] only some money—or some papers—that were lost in their case. But for us—!
          • 1918, Gunnar Heiberg, Samlede dramatiske verker, volume III, page 276:
            alle har set mine horn og jeg har dem ikke
            Everyone has seen my horns, and I do not have them.
          • 1992, Per Thomas Andersen, Arr, page 148:
            […] min svoger sa seg villig til å følge dem
            […] my brother-in-law agreed to accompany them.
        2. those; the object form of demonstrative de, often followed by a phrase or relative clause identifying the people or things concerned.
          Jeg vil heller ha dem som ligger øverst. ― I would rather have those on top.
          • 1882, Henrik Ibsen, En folkefiende, page 50:
            det er alle de rige, alle dem med de gamle ansete navne i byen … som styrer og råder over os
            It is all the rich, all those with the old respected names in town … who govern and rule over us.
          • 1882, Alexander Kielland, Skipper Worse, page 15:
            anskuelser og ideer, vidt forskjellige fra dem, med hvilke der arbeides i den tarvelige by
            Views and ideas very different from those with which people work in the modest town.
          • 1896, Lorentz Dietrichson, Svundne Tider, volume I, page 92:
            dem, der har anledning til at læse P.A. Jensens … optegnelser, vil jeg bede om unskyldning
            I would ask those who have the opportunity to read P. A. Jensen's … notes to excuse me.
          • 1904, Hans E. Kinck, Emigranter, page 35:
            hun var av dem som snakked slæbende
            She was one of those who spoke with a drawl.
          • 2004, Bertrand Besigye, Svastikastjernen, page 159:
            […] dem som forgifter den
            […] those who poison it
        3. (dialectal) they; used as the subject pronoun corresponding to standard de.
          I morgen kommer dem. ― They are coming tomorrow.
          • 1918, Halfdan Kjerulf, edited by Wladimir Moe, Av hans efterladte papirer 1847–1868, page 240:
            svenskerne er da som besatte ianledning af statholderen, som vi dræbte. Men dem faar taale det
            The Swedes are quite beside themselves over the governor whom we killed off. But they will have to put up with it.
        4. (obsolete) whom, which; a plural relative pronoun, chiefly introducing a supplementary relative clause, used as an object or after a preposition.
          Han skrev flere brev, dem jeg siden brente. ― He wrote several letters, which I later burned.
          • 1882, Alexander Kielland, Skipper Worse, page 66:
            [han kunne] ikke mer end fire eller fem skriftsteder udenad, dem han anvendte som det kunde falde sig
            [He knew] no more than four or five passages of Scripture by heart, which he used as occasion arose.
          • 1916, Tryggve Andersen, Samlede fortællinger, volume I, page 132:
            fra gangen hørtes drukkent spektakel fra kontoristerne og opvarterkonerne, til dem nyheden endnu ikke var kommet
            Drunken uproar could be heard from the clerks and serving women in the corridor, to whom the news had not yet come.
          • 1923, Henrik Wergeland, “For Almuen. Andet Hefte”, in Samlede skrifter‎, volume IV,1:
            […] og saaledes flere Tegn til Lidelser, dem de Lidende eller Klagende selv fordetmeste foranledige sig.
            […] and thus further signs of sufferings which the sufferers or complainants mostly bring upon themselves.
        Usage notes
        • In standard written Bokmål, de is normally the subject form and dem the object form, including after prepositions. Dialectal subject dem is also represented in literature.
        • Both de and dem are accepted in certain predicative, comparative, existential and cleft constructions, such as Det var de/dem (“It was them”) and Hun er eldre enn de/dem (“She is older than them”).[2]
        • When de(m) som … functions as an object or follows a preposition, both forms are accepted, although Språkrådet recommends dem. This also applies when som is omitted. When the whole phrase is the subject of the main clause, use de.[3]
        • The polite second-person form Dem (“you”) is capitalized and has a separate entry.

        Determiner

        dem

        1. (dialectal) those; used before a plural noun in place of demonstrative de.
          Jeg kjenner dem folka der. ― I know those people there.
          • 1975, Gunnar Bull Gundersen, Unnskyld hvis jeg forstyrrer, page 59:
            […] dem folka der oppe […]
            […] those people up there […]
          • 1976, Torfinn Haukås, Svindlere, page 139:
            […] dem grisene […]
            […] those pigs […]

        Article

        dem

        1. (dialectal) the; the plural definite article before an adjective or other modifier, corresponding to standard de.
          Jeg liker dem gamle husa. ― I like the old houses.
          • 1911, Amalie Pettersen, Pettersens, page 119:
            dem skotske rampeguttene skulde hat faddeleg juling, saan som dem frækket sig
            The Scottish rascals ought to have had a terrible beating, the way they behaved so cheekily.
          • 1952, Torborg Nedreaas, De varme hendene, page 199:
            […] dem andre butikkene
            […] the other shops

        Swedish

        Pronunciation

        • IPA(key): /ˈdɔmː/, (Finland Swedish) /ˈdɛmː/
        • (Standard Swedish) Homophone: de
        • Rhymes: -ɔmː, -ɛmː

        Pronoun

        dem (third-person plural)

        1. them; accusative/dative of de
          De ser dem
          They see them
        2. misspelling of de

        Usage notes

        In most dialects, de (“they”) and dem (“them”) are no longer distinguished in speech. They are regularly mixed up in writing by native speakers, due to lack of grammatical intuition. The article de is often mixed up with dem as well.
